title: Spinning Numbers
question: What kind of number could square to −1, and why would it wiggle?

blocks.text: Last time the spring needed a number with $a^2 = -4$. Theo said no such number exists. But what would one even *look* like?

Picture every number as an **arrow** from 0 along the number line. Multiplying by 2 stretches the arrow. Multiplying by ½ shrinks it. And multiplying by −1 flips it to point the other way. That's a **half turn**.
Ooh. If ×(−1) is a half turn… what's *half* of a half turn? A **quarter** turn! The arrow would point straight up, off the number line.
Let's give the quarter turn a name: **i**. Do it twice and you've done a half turn, which is ×(−1). So $i \cdot i = -1$. There's our number that squares to a negative!

blocks.tex: i^2 = -1 \qquad\text{(two quarter turns = a half turn)}

blocks.text: Hold on. These are the "imaginary numbers". Everyone knows they're made up. They can't describe a real, physical spring.
They're not imaginary, they're **sideways**! It's just a 2-D arrow. Turning left is as real as walking forward.
A number like $3 + 2i$ just means "3 steps along, 2 steps sideways". The whole plane of arrows is the stage for everything that follows.
The name "imaginary" started out as an insult, centuries ago, and it stuck. Don't let it fool you.
If i is a quarter turn, we're going to be spinning arrows all day. So how do we say *how much* an arrow has turned?

Degrees are an old habit: 360 of them in a turn, because an ancient calendar liked 360. Mathematicians measure a turn with the circle itself. Roll a wheel of radius 1 and see how far its rim travels. A **radian** is the angle whose arc is exactly **one radius** long.

blocks.q: How many radians make one full turn?

options.why: That's degrees. A radian is much bigger than a degree: about 57 of them.
Right. The whole rim of a radius-1 wheel is 2π ≈ 6.28 radii long, so a full turn is 2π radians. Half a turn is π ≈ 3.14.
One radian only rolls one radius of rim, about a sixth of the way round.

blocks.text: Follow the arrow's tip as it turns. Its shadow on the real axis is called the **cosine** of the angle, $\cos\theta$; its shadow on the sideways axis is the **sine**, $\sin\theta$. Turn steadily and both shadows trace waves, the sine a quarter turn behind the cosine.
Got it. So a spinner at 2 radians per second goes round twice a second!
Twice a second would be 2 turns, $4\pi$ radians. Two radians per second is one full turn every $2\pi/2 \approx 3.14$ seconds.

items.def: The angle whose arc is one radius long. A full turn is $2\pi$ radians, half a turn is $\pi$.
The shadows of a length-1 arrow at angle θ: $\cos\theta$ along the real axis, $\sin\theta$ sideways.

blocks.text: Speeds of turning are measured in radians per second: a spinner at 2 radians per second makes one full turn in $2\pi/2 \approx 3.14$ seconds. The symbol ω tells us that turning speed.

Now picture a point running around a circle at a steady speed, ω radians per second. Where does its **velocity** point? (Velocity is Chapter 3's speed with a direction, so a moving arrow's velocity is an arrow too: which way its tip moves, and how fast.) Always along the circle, which is a **quarter turn** ahead of the arrow to the point.
A quarter turn is ×i, and the speed is ω times the radius. So the velocity is the position turned a quarter turn, times ω: **velocity = iω × position**.
Wait. "The slope is a fixed number times itself" is exactly the **exponential** property from Chapter 4! With a = iω.
But hang on. In Chapter 4 a power meant "how much multiplying has happened". What would $e$ to the power $i\theta$ even mean? Multiply by $e$, $i\theta$ times?
Build it the Chapter 4 way. $e$ was $n$ tiny steps of growing by $\frac1n$. Make each tiny step a little nudge *sideways* instead.

Each step turns the arrow by a tiny angle, about $\theta/n$ radians, and stretches it a tiny bit. With more steps the stretching fades away and the path lands on the circle, exactly θ radians round. That's why radians: the tiny sideways nudges add up along the rim. So $e^{i\theta}$ is simply the point on the circle at angle θ.
So $e^{i\omega t}$ is not scary at all. It's a point **spinning** around the circle of radius 1, ω radians every second. Watch it, and watch its **shadow** on the real axis:

blocks.tex: \begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dt}\,e^{i\omega t} &= i\omega\,e^{i\omega t} \\ \text{shadow on the real axis} &= \cos(\omega t)\end{aligned}

blocks.text: The shadow slides back and forth as a perfect **cosine wave**. A spinning arrow, seen side-on, is a wiggle. That's where the wiggle has been hiding.
Written out in full, the spinner is $e^{i\omega t} = \cos\omega t + i\sin\omega t$: the along part is a cosine, the sideways part a sine. People call this Euler's formula.

items: Numbers are arrows. Multiplying rotates and stretches them. **i** is a quarter turn, so $i^2 = -1$.
A **radian** is the angle whose arc is one radius long: a full turn is $2\pi$. **cos θ** and **sin θ** are the shadows of a turned arrow.
$e^{i\theta}$, built from tiny sideways steps $\left(1 + \frac{i\theta}{n}\right)^n$, is the point on the circle at angle θ.
$e^{i\omega t}$ is a point spinning around a circle. Its shadow is a cosine wave.
A spinner's velocity is always a quarter turn ahead of its position: velocity $= i\omega \times$ position. That's the exponential rule with $a = i\omega$.

items.q: What does multiplying the arrow 3 by i, twice, give?

options.why: Two quarter turns are a half turn: 3 → 3i → −3.
That's after *one* quarter turn. Do it once more.
Multiplying by i turns the arrow. It doesn't change its length.

items.q: A spinner turns at ω = π radians per second. How long does one full turn take?

options.why: A full turn is 2π radians. At π radians per second that takes 2π ÷ π = 2 seconds.
π is how many radians it covers each second, not how long a turn takes.
One second covers π radians: only half a turn.

items.q: Which way does the velocity of the spinner $e^{i\omega t}$ point?

options.text: A quarter turn ahead of its position arrow, along the circle
options.why: Velocity $= i\omega \times$ position, and $\times i$ is a quarter turn. The push is always sideways, so the point never gets closer to the centre or further away: it just goes round.
Then the point would fall inwards and the arrow would shrink. A quarter-turn push keeps it on the circle.

options.text: Straight out, along the position arrow
options.why: That's $e^{at}$ with a real, positive $a$: it grows. With $a = i\omega$ the push is sideways.

blocks.text: Mika: "So the spring's mystery number exists after all: it's 2i. Does that mean a real spring swings **sideways**?"

rotate.title: Multiplying turns arrows
rotate.start: Start with the arrow 3. Try the buttons!
rotate.tooBig: That would go off the page. Try another button.

explain.two: ×2 stretches the arrow to twice the length. Same direction.
explain.half: ×½ shrinks it to half the length. Same direction.
explain.neg: ×(−1) is a half turn: the arrow flips to point the other way.
explain.i: ×i is a quarter turn, counter-clockwise. Do it twice and compare with ×(−1)!

rotate.aria: A plane with an arrow from the origin. Buttons multiply the arrow by 2, one half, minus one or i, rotating or stretching it.

turns.title: Measuring turns in radii
turns.aria: A circle of radius 1 with an arrow at angle theta, its arc highlighted, and the arrow tip's shadows on both axes.
turns.plotAria: The cosine and sine of the angle, traced from 0 up to the chosen angle.
turns.oneRadian: One radian: the arc is exactly one radius long (about 57°).
turns.half: Half a turn: π ≈ 3.14 radians. The shadows are at −1 and 0.
turns.full: A full turn: 2π ≈ 6.28 radians, back where we started.
turns.help: Slide θ. The orange arc is the distance rolled along the rim, measured in radii.

tiny.title: Turning in tiny sideways steps
tiny.aria: The partial products of 1 plus i theta over n, drawn as a path from 1 towards the point on the unit circle at angle theta.
tiny.one: One giant step: 1 + iθ, far off the circle (length {len}).
tiny.many: {n} steps: length {len}, angle {ang} rad. More steps: the length creeps to 1 and the angle to θ = {th}.
tiny.help: Slide n to cut the turn into more, smaller nudges; slide θ to change where it is heading.

spinner.title: The spinner and its shadow
spinner.help: The velocity arrow (drawn shorter to fit) always points a quarter turn ahead of the position arrow. The blue dot on the real axis is the shadow.
spinner.aria: A point spinning around a circle, with its position arrow, a velocity arrow a quarter turn ahead, and its shadow on the real axis.
spinner.plotAria: The shadow of the spinner over time: a cosine wave.
